questiontext.text:
River pollution and distance downstream

An environmental scientist collected water samples at 20 sites downstream from a pollution source to investigate the relationship between distance and pollutant concentration.

Download the dataset. It contains four columns:

  • Site: the sampling-site identifier.
  • Distance_downstream_km: distance from the pollution source, in kilometres.
  • Recorded_concentration: the pollutant concentration reported by the laboratory.
  • Unit: the measurement unit for the corresponding concentration.

Download pollution_data.csv

Calculate Pearson's correlation coefficient between distance downstream and pollutant concentration. Give your answer to three decimal places.

\(r=\) [[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]]

How would you describe the relationship between the two variables?

[[input:ans2]] [[validation:ans2]]

generalfeedback.text:
Key lesson

Before calculating statistics, always check the meaning and units of your data. A column containing numerical values is not necessarily ready for analysis.

Inconsistent units can produce a convincing but completely misleading correlation coefficient.

prtcorrect.text: Correct answer, well done.

prtpartiallycorrect.text: Your answer is partially correct.

prtincorrect.text: Incorrect answer.

truefeedback.text:
Correct! You have accounted for the differences in units before calculating the correlations

If you did not clean the data, and just used the concentration values exactly as recorded in the file, it would indicate a strong positive linear relationship: pollutant concentration seems to increase with distance downstream.

[[jsxgraph width="500px" height="350px"]] var xs = {#distances#}; var ys = {#recorded_conc#}; var xmin = Math.min.apply(null, xs); var xmax = Math.max.apply(null, xs); var ymin = 0; var ymax = Math.max.apply(null, ys); var xpad = (xmax-xmin)*0.1; var ypad = ymax*0.1; var board = JXG.JSXGraph.initBoard(divid, { boundingbox: [ xmin-xpad, ymax+ypad, xmax+xpad, -ypad ], axis: true, showCopyright: false, showNavigation: false }); for (var i=0; i ● Blue: measurements recorded in mg/L.
● Red: measurements recorded in µg/L.

Notice how the measurements recorded in µg/L appear much larger simply because they are expressed in a different unit.

After expressing all concentrations in mg/L, Pearson's correlation becomes

\[ r={@r_clean_display@}. \]

as you correctly identified! It is then a strong negative linear relationship. Pollutant concentration generally decreases as distance downstream increases.

After converting every concentration to mg/L, the scatterplot reveals the underlying relationship.

[[jsxgraph width="500px" height="350px"]] var xs = {#distances#}; var ys = {#clean_conc#}; var xmin = Math.min.apply(null, xs); var xmax = Math.max.apply(null, xs); var ymin = Math.min.apply(null, ys); var ymax = Math.max.apply(null, ys); var xpad = (xmax-xmin)*0.1; var ypad = Math.max((ymax-ymin)*0.1, 0.5); var board = JXG.JSXGraph.initBoard(divid, { boundingbox: [ xmin-xpad, ymax+ypad, xmax+xpad, ymin-ypad ], axis: true, showCopyright: false, showNavigation: false }); for (var i=0; i The data now show a strong negative linear relationship. The pollutant concentration generally decreases with distance downstream.

Notice: No observations were removed. The measurements have simply been expressed in consistent units.

Why did the relationship reverse?

Pearson's correlation is sensitive to unusually large numerical values. In this dataset, the inconsistent measurement units created artificially large values in the concentration column.

Because those values occurred at sampling sites farther downstream, the unconverted data appeared to show an increasing trend.

Your coefficient matches the result obtained by using the recorded concentration values exactly as they appear in the dataset.

However, there is something important about these measurements that you may have overlooked.

Examine the columns carefully. Are all the concentration values directly comparable?

The distance column is expressed consistently in kilometres. However, the concentration column contains measurements recorded in two different units:

  • Milligrams per litre (mg/L)
  • Micrograms per litre (µg/L)

These values cannot be compared directly without converting them to a common unit.

There are 1000 micrograms in one milligram. Therefore,

\[ 1\text{ mg/L}=1000\text{ µg/L}. \]

To express all concentrations in mg/L, divide every value recorded in µg/L by 1000.

Why not try plotting your two variables in a scatter plot to see if it still looks right?

falsefeedback.text: Your correlation coefficient is not correct. Check which columns you have used and whether the values are suitable for direct comparison.

truefeedback.text: Your interpretation is consistent with the coefficient you calculated.
